title: LinkedIn for High Schoolers
subtitle: An example profile you can build without a job or a founder title, section by section, plus a first message to send.
fromVideo: From the video: what to put on LinkedIn in high school
intro: Meet Jordan, a made-up junior with no job and no club title. Every example below is Jordan's. Anything in [brackets] is yours to swap. You have to be 16 to make a LinkedIn account.

entries.title: Use a clear, recent photo of your face
entries.lead: A school portrait or a photo against a plain wall works.
items: Make sure your face is easy to see, with no filters and no group shots.
The cover photo behind it is optional. A picture of your school or something you made is fine.
entries.note: LinkedIn's student page says you don't need a professional headshot, just a clear, recent photo that looks like you.

entries.title: Start the headline with your grade and school
entries.lead: Jordan's headline reads “Junior at [your school] | Interested in [graphic design] | Volunteer at [Riverside Library]”.
items: Your grade and school tell people where to place you.
Then add the thing you're working on, or one interest if you haven't started anything yet.
Keep titles you earned, like club president. Leave out ones you didn't.
entries.note: LinkedIn's student page suggests pairing the experience you already have with the field you want to explore next.

entries.title: Use the About to explain what your headline names
entries.lead: Write two to four sentences in your own voice. If your headline says robotics, this is where you describe the robot you built.
items: Jordan's About says “I'm a junior at [your school] who likes design. This year I made the flyers for our school food drive and taught myself the basics of Canva. On weekends I help kids with reading at [Riverside Library]. I'd like to learn how designers land their first projects.”
Say what you like doing and what you've tried so far. Leave out phrases like “passionate about making an impact.”
entries.note: LinkedIn suggests keeping the About to one or two paragraphs.

entries.title: Pin one thing you made in Featured
entries.lead: Featured sits above your Activity section and stays hidden until you add something.
items: Jordan pinned a photo of the food drive flyer.
A class project, a slideshow, a video or a link to a post all work.
One good item beats five weak ones.

entries.title: Put anything people counted on you for in Experience
entries.lead: You don't need a formal job. You do need to label each entry honestly.
items: Jordan lists “Babysitter, Self-employed” with one line on what it involves, like watching two kids two afternoons a week and handling school pickups.
A part-time job, helping at a family business and regular paid gigs all belong here.
Volunteering has its own Volunteering section. A club you lead can go here or under Organizations, as long as you say what you did.
Never mark a school activity as Full-time.
entries.note: LinkedIn says Experience entries must be accurately labeled, and it uses Full-time for roles that take all of someone's professional time.

entries.title: Keep Education and Skills short
entries.lead: List your high school and the year you expect to graduate. Add summer programs you finished.
items: Add coursework only if it explains your interest.
For skills, pick a few you could explain if someone asked. Jordan added Canva, Google Slides and Spanish.
Skip broad traits like “hardworking.” Your examples show those.

entries.title: Send one specific question when you connect
entries.lead: Find someone whose work looks interesting, like an alum from your school, and add a note to your connection request.
items: Jordan's note says “Hi [Name], I'm a [junior] at [your school] too. I saw you went into [design]. What was the first [project you put in your portfolio]?”
Change every bracket. Ask about something they did, so the answer takes a minute, not an hour.
Ask about their path, not for a job.
On a free account you can add a note to three connection requests a month, up to 200 characters each. You can only message people you're connected with.
entries.note: Filled in, Jordan's note is well under 200 characters.

entries.title: If you're under 18, check your message settings
entries.lead: LinkedIn lets you choose to receive messages only from your connections.
items: LinkedIn says this keeps recruiters and other members from contacting you.
Only connect with people you've met or can tell are real professionals, like alumni and teachers.

rule.title: The short version
items: Grade, school and one interest in the headline
What you're into and what you've tried in the About
One thing you made in Featured
Anything people counted on you for in Experience
One specific question in your first note

verifyNote: LinkedIn rules checked live on LinkedIn Help (answers a563153, a6239760, 62940, a552452, a554351, a593695, a554472), students.linkedin.com and the User Agreement on 2026-11-22. Jordan is a made-up example.
